title: Develop Your Pieces
subtitle: Get knights and bishops out fast, toward the center.
goals: Don't move the same piece twice

steps.say: Take control of the game by developing your pieces rapidly to squares where they control the center. Every move in the opening should bring a new piece into play — the army that mobilizes first gets to attack first.

steps.prompt: Develop a knight toward the center — with a threat!
hints: The best developing moves do two jobs: bring a piece out AND create a threat.
Which knight jump attacks Black's e5 pawn?

line.say: Great choice! This is by far the most popular move by top players in this position — it develops AND attacks the e5 pawn.

rejections.say: A healthy developing move — but Nf3 does strictly more: it develops AND attacks e5, forcing Black to respond.
The queen ventures out far too early — Black will develop pieces while chasing her, gaining time for free.
A knight on the rim is dim! From h3 it touches no central squares. Knights belong on f3 and c3.

steps.wrongSay: Develop a KNIGHT — to the square where it eyes the center and attacks e5.
steps.successSay: Develop with threats and your opponent spends their moves reacting to you.

steps.prompt: White attacks your e5 pawn. How can Black develop a knight to defend the pawn?
hints: Defend AND develop in the same move — that's the efficient way.

line.say: Perfect — the knight defends e5 and takes its best square, all in one move. Problem solved for free.

rejections.say: That's the Petrov — a real opening that counter-attacks e4 instead of defending. But the task here: defend e5 WITH A KNIGHT. Nc6 does it.
It defends the pawn, but with a pawn move that blocks your dark-squared bishop — and the question asked for a knight. Develop while defending!
The queen defends e5 but blocks her own bishop and stands awkwardly. Save the queen for later — knights first.

steps.wrongSay: e5 needs a defender — and one of your knights can do it while developing.
steps.successSay: One move, two jobs. That efficiency is the whole art of the opening.

steps.prompt: Develop your bishop to attack a black knight.
hints: Which black knight can a bishop reach — and what is that knight doing?
The c6 knight defends e5. Pressure IT and you pressure the pawn behind it.

line.say: The Ruy Lopez! The bishop pressures the c6 knight — the defender of e5 — so your attack on the pawn grows indirectly. Development with venom.

rejections.say: The Italian Game — excellent development toward f7. But the task was to attack a KNIGHT: Bb5 hits the defender of e5.
Developed... barely. On e2 the bishop stares at its own pawns. Bishops want active diagonals with targets.

steps.wrongSay: One bishop move attacks a black knight directly. Look at the queenside diagonal.
steps.successSay: Attacking the defender — pressure doesn't always have to be direct.

steps.prompt: How should you free your queenside bishop to develop?
hints: The c1 bishop is walled in by its own d2 pawn. A pawn move opens the door — but which one is safe?
Count the defenders of d4 before charging two squares. One modest step does the job.

line.say: Exactly right — the humble d3 opens the c1 bishop's diagonal, supports e4, and hangs nothing. Quiet moves win games too.

rejections.say: Black wins a pawn! After exd4, e5, the c5-bishop and c6-knight all gang up on d4 — if Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4, then Bxd4 wins your queen. Try to find a safer pawn move to free your queenside bishop.
The fianchetto dream — but on b2 the bishop would bite on the well-defended e5 pawn. d3 frees the bishop toward g5 AND supports your center.

steps.wrongSay: Free the c1 bishop with a pawn move — the one that doesn't drop material.
steps.successSay: Before every pawn push, count the attackers on the square it crosses. d4 was a trap; d3 was the move.

steps.prompt: Develop your bishop and attack their knight!
hints: Only one of your bishops still sits at home — and it just got its diagonal opened.
Send it to the square where it pins the f6 knight against the queen.

line.say: Development with a PIN — the f6 knight now can't move without losing the queen behind it. Your last minor piece joined the game with maximum effect.

rejections.say: It develops, but attacks no knight — and invites Bxe3, helping Black trade. The aggressive square is on the kingside.
That bishop is already developed — moving it again attacks c6, but wastes time. Develop the NEW piece: the c1 bishop can attack a knight too.

steps.wrongSay: The c1 bishop is finally free — find the square where it develops AND hits a knight.
steps.successSay: All minor pieces out, a pin on the board, castling next — that's a textbook opening.
